title: The Daegu Shop Lee Byung-chul Opened After Losing His Masan Land
dek: In 1938, after war wrecked his land deals in Masan, Lee Byung-chul started again with a trading shop in Daegu called Samsung Sanghoe.

story.event: Starting a Daegu trading shop after his Masan rice mill and land business collapsed
story.summary: In spring 1936 Lee Byung-chul went into a rice mill in Masan, then added a transport business and bought farmland on bank credit; when the Sino-Japanese War broke out in 1937, land prices fell, banks called in loans and he sold up to clear his debts. After about two months of travel he opened Samsung Sanghoe in Daegu on 1 March 1938 with 30,000 won, trading produce and dried fish to China and Manchuria and later making Star-brand noodles. He later called the collapse a painful but precious lesson.
paragraphs: On 1 March 1938, Lee Byung-chul opened a trading shop in Su-dong, a neighbourhood near Seomun market in Daegu, under a sign reading Samsung Sanghoe. Samsung means three stars. It was his second start in two years.

The first had been in Masan. In the spring of 1936 he went into a rice mill there with partners, using land he had inherited from his father as his stake. The mill made money, and he added a transport business. Then he borrowed from banks to buy farmland, and within about a year, Daegu's Maeil Shinmun reported, he held some two million pyeong, roughly 660 hectares. When war broke out between Japan and China in 1937, land prices fell and the banks began calling in their loans. He sold the mill and the transport firm to clear his debts.

What he did next was slower. He spent about two months travelling, through Korea and into China, looking at markets before he chose again. He settled on trade: it needed relatively little capital, and under Japanese rule Manchuria was short of dried fish and vegetables. He picked Daegu for its place at the centre of the Yeongnam region, with farm produce flowing in and a railway running through, and started with 30,000 won.

Samsung Sanghoe bought fruit and vegetables from around Daegu and dried fish from Pohang and other ports, and shipped them to China and Manchuria. It also installed milling and noodle machines. Its Star-brand noodles cost a little more than its rivals' but, by the Maeil Shinmun's account, sold best of the city's five noodle makers. In 1939 he bought a brewery, and by 1941, when the business was incorporated, it had about 40 staff. In 1947 he moved it to Seoul.

Lee later called the Masan collapse a "painful but precious lesson". The rules he drew from it were about his own conduct rather than the war: watch for change at home and abroad, give up reckless greed, do not speculate on luck, and have another plan ready for a crisis.

quote.text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: Lee had an obvious culprit in the war, which no trader in Masan could have stopped. The rules he took from the loss pointed at his own speculation instead. The verse explains why that is rarer than it sounds: our own share is the part we are best at hiding.

reflection: When something you have built goes wrong, there is usually a real outside cause: a funder who changed course, a supplier who let you down, a season that went badly. Naming it is honest. Stopping there is comfortable.

Lee's war was real. What he carried forward, though, was the part he could change: the speculation he had run on borrowed money. He also took two months before he chose again, which looks less like delay than like part of the repair. A loss tends to ask for both: a plain account of your own share, and enough time before the next decision.
invitation: Think of one recent thing that went worse than you hoped. Write one sentence about the outside cause and one about your own part, then leave both until you are rested enough to read them kindly.

sources.supports: Spring 1936 rice mill in Masan with inherited farmland as capital; transport business; bank-financed land purchases reaching about two million pyeong; the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese War making the bank loans a problem; travel in Korea and China before choosing trade; reasons for choosing Daegu (centre of Yeongnam, hub for produce, railway); opening on 1 March 1938 in Su-dong (now Ingyo-dong); produce from around Daegu and dried fish from Pohang exported to China and Manchuria; milling and noodle machines and Star-brand (Byeolpyo) noodles, dearer but the most successful of Daegu's five noodle factories; brewery bought within a year; incorporation in 1941 with about 40 employees.

cross_checks.claim: Samsung Sanghoe opened in Daegu on 1 March 1938.
Lee's first business, a rice mill in Masan begun in 1936, was wound up after the Sino-Japanese War broke out in 1937.
The collapse came through land bought on bank credit: prices fell and loans were called in, and he sold the mill and transport business to pay his debts.
The Daegu business started with 30,000 won.
Samsung Sanghoe traded dried fish and produce to China and Manchuria and made noodles.
Lee travelled for about two months, including in China, before choosing trade and Daegu.

research_notes: Lee's own memoir (Hoam Jajeon, 1986) is the root source for most of this episode but no full text is online; the National Assembly Library catalogue shows chapters on starting in rice milling and transport and on becoming a landlord of two million pyeong, which matches the Maeil Shinmun accounts. The bank-loan and land detail (about two million pyeong, prices falling, loans recalled, mill and transport firm sold) comes from Daegu's Maeil Shinmun (2010 and 2014, same publisher); Aju Business Daily independently says the war forced him into liquidation and that his trouble lay in speculation, and Korea JoongAng Daily says his finances worsened after the war began. Aju's 'short-sight' verdict is the reporter's, so the story uses only the phrase Aju attributes to Lee himself ('painful but precious lesson') and his principles as Aju reports them. Age at founding differs (Maeil: 28 full years; Aju: 29; Lankov: 'exactly 30', probably Korean age), so the story gives none. Where the 30,000 won came from differs: Lankov says it was given by his family; Maeil (2014) says he moved to Daegu with what remained after clearing his debts; the story gives the sum without its origin. Aju's account of his travel route ('from Busan to Pyeongyang through Shanghai') is garbled in translation; the story says only 'through Korea and into China' (Maeil 2010) for about two months (Aju). Gale's International Directory of Company Histories (encyclopedia.com) places the rice mill in Taegu and the early trade in wool and textiles; it conflicts with every Korean source and was not used. The building is described by Maeil as a four-storey wooden shop with a basement, while JoongAng Daily calls it a small store; the story avoids describing its size. The Masan mill's partner is named in Lee's memoir as Park Jeong-won, according to a 2023 report on a 1938 Japanese directory (twig24.com); the story says only 'with partners'. Two million pyeong converts to about 6.6 million square metres, roughly 660 hectares. The verse is applied by analogy.
